title: Script Process

source.quote: Study of the life-script has revealed a fascinating fact. It is that there seem to be only six main patterns of script process.

setting: Saturday night, a housewarming party. Sam is the kind of friend people end up talking to for a while.

L1.line: Once the kitchen's actually finished - not just 'mostly' finished, I mean properly done - then I'll finally sit down and relax.
cues: the word 'once' doing double duty, twice over
no mention yet of when 'then' might actually arrive
L1.question: Quick primer: a 'script process pattern' isn't about what someone's story is, but its timing shape - Until, After, Never, Always, Almost, or Open-ended - how a life (or even one sentence) decides when good things are finally 'allowed' to happen. Which script process pattern is Teodora's sentence structure itself demonstrating?

options.text: After - she's setting up to pay for today's pleasure tomorrow.
options.feedback: After has its own tell: a 'high,' then a hard 'but,' then a 'low' ('great party, but I'll regret it tomorrow'). There's no high here at all yet - everything is deferred forward, not paid for backward.

options.text: Until - nothing good can happen until something less-good is finished first.
options.feedback: Right - and the sentence does it too: she interrupts herself to add one more condition before she'll let herself get to the relaxing part. The structure enacts the belief.

options.text: Always - the same unsatisfying thing keeps repeating.
options.feedback: Always shows up as tangents and repetition ('what I'm trying to tell you is... oh, and by the way...'). This sentence is linear and single-pointed, just endlessly gated.

options.text: Open-ended - there's no plan for what happens after the goal.
options.feedback: Open-ended's tell is a void after the finish line, not a gate before it. Teodora has a very clear 'then' - she's just never finished qualifying what counts as 'done.'

L1.lesson: Script process patterns show up in sentence structure, not just life events. The parenthetical self-interruption ('not just mostly finished, I mean properly done') is Until playing out in miniature, in real time, inside a single sentence.

L2.intro: Two friends, two patterns, same party.

beats.line: This is such a great night! ...but my head is going to be killing me tomorrow, I just know it.
cues: high energy on the first half
already resigned to the hangover before it's happened

options.text: Yeah, enjoy it while it lasts, I guess.
options.outcome: Yusuf nods, a little too readily, and orders another round 'to get it in before the crash.'
options.lesson: Sympathetic agreement still colludes with the sword-of-Damocles framing - even kindly meant, it confirms that tonight has to be paid for tomorrow.

options.text: What if tonight didn't have to cost you tomorrow? Pace yourself and you might get both.
options.outcome: Yusuf laughs. 'Wait, that's allowed?' He switches to water for a round, genuinely surprised at the idea.
options.lesson: The real antidote to an After pattern is concrete and behavioral - decide to enjoy tomorrow too, before tonight, then act accordingly. Not advice to relax; a specific move.

options.text: Don't worry about tomorrow, that's such an Always thing to say.
options.outcome: Yusuf looks confused. 'That's not really what I meant, though.'
options.lesson: Script process patterns are specific - naming the wrong one (Always instead of After) misses the actual lever, even when the instinct to name a pattern at all was right.

options.text: Ugh, same old Yusuf, you always do this.
options.outcome: Yusuf's face falls a little. 'Okay, sorry for having a good time,' he says, and the night sours.
options.lesson: Naming someone's pattern from Parent judgment invites defensiveness, not insight - the difference between diagnosing with someone and diagnosing at them.

beats.line: I keep meaning to update my resume. I will, though - definitely, maybe next week.
cues: roughly the same sentence as last month
no concrete next step attached to 'will'
says it almost cheerfully, like it's not really a problem

options.text: Why haven't you done it yet?
options.outcome: Lina gives another perfectly reasonable excuse. Nothing changes.
options.lesson: Content-level questions don't touch a Never script - there's always a plausible reason, and that's the point of the pattern, not a flaw in it.

options.text: Let's pick one concrete thing you could do about it - this week, right now.
options.outcome: Lina blinks, then actually names one real, small action - and looks oddly relieved to have been asked that way.
options.lesson: The step out of Never is almost absurdly concrete: name the want, list five small actions, do one. It breaks Tantalus's stillness by making the next step too small to defer.

options.text: Maybe you don't actually want a new job.
options.outcome: Lina gets defensive - maybe it's true, maybe it isn't, but it lands as a guess dressed up as insight.
options.lesson: It's tempting to interpret the motive behind a Never pattern; often the simpler, more useful move is just asking for the next concrete step.

options.text: You'll get there eventually, don't stress about it.
options.outcome: Lina relaxes, relieved - and nothing about this week changes either.
options.lesson: Reassurance that removes urgency can feed a Never pattern instead of interrupting it: it confirms that no step is needed right now, which is exactly the belief keeping Tantalus still.

fields.label: Which of the six process patterns - Until, After, Never, Always, Almost, Open-ended - fits a day in your own life best? Name one concrete, specific behavior (not just 'relax more') that would break it.

echo.setting: A month later. Sam, scrolling their own calendar at 11pm.
echo.line: Sam catches themselves thinking 'I'll relax once this week calms down' - the same thing they thought about last week, and the week before that.
